actions.reason: BasicTokenizer.train holds token ids as one character per id. New tokens used chr(256 + i), so after the first merge the ids str widened to 2 bytes per character. From then on every split had to re-check and narrow each part, every join copied twice the bytes, and every neighbour character above U+00FF pulled out of a part was a new str allocation. New tokens now take byte values that never occur in the training text, while any remain, and fall back to chr(256 + i) after that. This keeps ids at 1 byte per character, and neighbour characters come from the cached 1-byte character singletons. A small char -> id dict maps these characters back to token ids when recording the merge pair. The invariant the update logic relies on still holds: the minted character never occurs in ids before the merge. Tie-breaking is unchanged because it uses ids.find over pair positions, which does not depend on which character stands for a token, so outputs stay identical.

journal.text:
I tried to keep the token id string narrow in BasicTokenizer.train in minbpe/basic.py. It holds one character per id. New tokens used chr(256 + i), so after the first merge the str widened to 2 bytes per character. Every split then re-checked and narrowed parts, every join copied twice the bytes, and neighbour characters above U+00FF were new allocations. I changed new tokens to take byte values that do not occur in the text. That meant three edits in basic.py, 15 changed lines.

The sandbox run was accepted with identical outputs. train_basic_ir went from 264603878 to 261683692, ratio 0.9890. The other metrics moved up slightly: train_regex_ir 1.0024, encode_ir 1.0043, decode_ir 1.0040, save_load_ir 1.0020. All guards were within limits.

The gain is small. Str width is not the main cost in train. The pair counting and merge loop likely dominate.

Next I will profile the counting step in train and look at the drift in encode_ir, which I did not touch.
